meaningMnemonic: This radical is the same as the kanji. It means anti . Just in case you don't remember this, here's the kanji meaning mnemonic: The stool ( 又 ) is in the cliff ( 厂 ). If someone has a stool deep inside a cliff, they are most likely pretty anti society, hiding away like that.
This radical kind of looks like a brush . The top part is a hand holding the brush handle, and the bottom part is the bristly tip.
This radical looks like a curvy letter B. What does B stand for? Building ! This radical often shows up in kanji related to gatherings or to places where people come together… like buildings.

There's the bottom of a shoe with spikes coming out of it. Only one kind of shoe is like this, and that's a cleat . You know, like those studded shoes athletes wear. Soccer cleats, baseball cleats, running cleats… You knew they were called cleats, right?

A clown face, with the funny hat at the top, the silly eyes in the middle, and the big laughing mouth at the bottom. This thing is pretty cute, unlike a lot of clowns… You could also see this as the stand radical on top of the mouth radical, since standing on their mouth is the kind of weird trick a clown would do.
See all the arms sticking out of this radical? Those are for hanging lots of coats and things on, because this is a coat rack . Kind of a weird coat rack, but definitely a coat rack.

You're lost, but you've come across a signpost that says " correct " in all directions. "Correct," "correct," "correct," it says. No matter which way you go, it's the correct way! What a relief! You could also use the mnemonic you learned with the kanji: There is a line on the ground so you stop, making a giant sign pop up that says CORRECT! You obeyed the rules of the road and did the correct thing. Good on you.

A drop of water will last for an eternity . Especially if you drop it into an endless stream that never stops flowing. You can see these streams converging from all directions here, flowing for eternity.

Someone shoved horns onto your husband and said he has to fight for them now. They turned him into a gladiator ! Now your husband has to fight for their amusement. Are you not entertained?! P.S. You know this is a gladiator, not a viking, because the horns are on the gladiator's shoulder pads instead of his helmet, and his helmet has a big crest on it.

This is the heavy radical. See the square fist in the center, grasping the handle of a dumbbell that has two heavy plates on the top and bottom? The radical just looks like it would be heavy, you know?

This radical looks like a helicopter coming straight at you, doesn't it? You can't see the tail part because it's behind the bigger front cab of the helicopter. But you can see the front windows and the big spinning blade on top.
This is the history radical. You can see a textbook and a couple crossed swords. Because that's basically how history works — fight battles, record the results, and do it all over again. History!

This radical looks like a hat with some legs under it. If all you can see is legs, the person wearing the hat must really be jammed in there. Have you ever tried to cram yourself into a hat so hard it covers your body? Yeah, didn't think so. But imagine how jammed in to that hat you'd be if you did.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means machine . Just in case you don't remember this, here's the kanji meaning mnemonic: You have a private mouth that's a machine . But you have to keep your machine mouth private because it would scare all the non-machine people around you.
This is the spicy radical. See how it's wide at the top, with a little stem sticking up, and narrow at the bottom? Just like a chili pepper. It's so spicy it can't even handle its own heat!

This is the spring radical, because it looks like a new plant shoot has pushed its way up through layers of dirt, snow, and ice to announce the coming of spring. Spring is the season (and the radical) full of new, growing life!
See the squid shape here? There's its pointy head, its eyes, and its tentacles (two, anyway). Pretty squid-like if you ask me!
Kind of a strange tent , I'll admit, but one that will protect you from things trying to get in (that's why it has all the spikes). It's the best you can do, considering you're in a cloth tent.

There's a canopy with a grid-like frame near the top. It's a yurt with a window! Yurts are those dome-shaped huts nomads use. Once you've set up a canopy with a window frame, you've basically built one. Imagine gazing out that window, kicking back in your yurt. Yurt sweet yurt!

Someone throws a cleat at your forehead while you sit on a stool . You must accept this. Then another guy cleats you in the forehead, but you remain on the stool and receive it without complaint. This is some kind of acceptance ritual for the most prestigious Spanish soccer club in the world. If a cleat to the forehead doesn't knock you off the stool, you'll receive an offer to join. Hints You're dealing with a lot of emotions right now. You feel the pain from being cleated in the forehead, but you're also glad to have finally been accepted into the soccer club. Suppress your pain and receive this honor.
readingMnemonic: After they accept you, they give you a small ju ice ( じゅ ) box. It's to help you recover from the trauma of getting kicked. And you receive the juice with grace. Hints Did you ever play soccer as a kid? Do you remember accepting a small juice box into your little kid hands during halftime? Apparently pros drink the same ones.

meaningMnemonic: A sheep that's big is a true beauty . Big is beautiful , and that's all the more true for sheep. Hints Imagine a great big beautiful sheep. See the sheep's beauty. This sheep is so big and fluffy that you can't see its tail, which is why it looks bit different in this kanji.
readingMnemonic: The big sheep's beauty has attracted a swarm of bee s ( び ). The sheep is so beautiful that the bees have mistaken it for a flower. Hints The bees are swarming around the sheep, marvelling at its beauty and trying to figure out how to get nectar from it.

meaningMnemonic: What does your mama tell you to do in the street ? Look before you cross! You gotta do it beforehand , or it could be too late. Hints Imagine yourself about to cross the street, and your mama saying in your ear: "always look beforehand"!
readingMnemonic: As you look beforehand , you see a yo- yo ( よ ) lying in the street. Hints As you cross the road, you pick up the yo-yo and put it in your pocket. You're really glad you looked beforehand, because you now have a yo-yo!

meaningMnemonic: Take the moon stamp on the stool in front of you and use it on all of your clothes . Now even if you sell or lose a piece of clothing , you'll be able to find it again by checking for your special moon stamp. Hints Imagine placing each piece of clothing you own onto the stool and carefully stamping them with a symbol of the moon. This should stop people from stealing all of your clothes!
readingMnemonic: A few days later you're with a friend when you recognize the clothes they're wearing. You grab it, rip it off, and scream, " F**k ( ふく ) you!" There is your moon stamp! These are your clothes!! Hints Your friend turns red and tries to pull the clothes back, "F**k you!" they yell. "No, f**k you, these are my clothes and I have proof this time!"

meaningMnemonic: The compare radical and the compare kanji are exactly the same! Huzzah!
readingMnemonic: Compare the he at ( ひ ) today with the heat yesterday. Is it hotter today? It's up to you to compare. Hints Feel today's heat. Now compare it to yesterday. You might want to check your thermometer if you're not sure!

meaningMnemonic: A yurt 's stool is always placed at certain degree s. The degrees change depending on specific occurrence s. Hints Since a yurt is round, the stool has to be angled at certain degrees. It's part of yurt culture. Imagine someone adjusting the stool with a measurement tool to adjust it to an exact degree.
readingMnemonic: Also angled at exact degree s is the do g ( ど ). Hints The dog changes its degrees at every occurrence of the stool changing. Picture the dog leaning at the exact degree the stool is at.

meaningMnemonic: Go to the tent and take the lantern from it, then we will be ready for departure . We can't leave the lantern inside of the tent; that's a fire hazard. We'd best take it with us before the departure. Don't you agree? Hints Feel the heat from the lantern. It's not quite as comforting as being inside a tent, but it's better than nothing. The lantern will light your way on your departure.
readingMnemonic: Oh! Don't forget your hats ( はつ ) either. Wouldn’t want to start a departure without hats or a lantern. That'd be a short journey. Hints How cold and unprotected would your head be without a hat? Very. Taking hats along with departures is integral to their success. Imagine how unsafe you would feel with no hats. That's no departure I want to set out on.

meaningMnemonic: You build a roof over your coat rack because you determine that this is the best way to protect your coats from the elements. Hints Think back on all the experiments and calculations you did to determine this. You tested all kinds of things — umbrellas, awnings, tarps — but ultimately you determined that only a roof would suffice.
readingMnemonic: Why did you determine your coat rack needed a roof? Because your coat pockets are full of ta ter ( てい ) tots! You can't afford to let your tater tots get rained on, so you determined they needed to be properly sheltered with a roof. Hints Stick your hands into your coat pockets and feel those crispy, toasty taters. You're not gonna let them come to any harm.

meaningMnemonic: If your rib cage is suddenly kick ed you'll probably want to express something. Anger or surprise, I'm guessing. At any rate a lot will get expressed on the surface of your face. Hints Imagine taking a kick to the rib cage out of nowhere. Ow. Okay, now how would you express yourself to your attacker? Maybe show it on the surface, wear your heart on your sleeve? Or pretend it didn't bother you?
readingMnemonic: The only thing you can think to express is " Heyo " ( ひょう )! Kind of a cross between "hey" and "yo." Like "heyo, stop it!" It doesn't really match the moment, but it's how you expressed yourself. Hints Imagine yourself saying it more like ひょう , though. ひょう , stop it! Hm… Maybe you should express yourself through retributive violence or something instead.

meaningMnemonic: Under your roof in winter there are more mouth s to feed because you let guest s stay with you when it's cold. Some of them aren't family, so they have to pay to stay under your roof and get food. Those are customer s. Hints Picture all of the hungry guests and customers under your roof, eating your food and sleeping on your floor.
readingMnemonic: One of your guest s is a regular named Kyaku ( きゃく ) the customer . Kyaku is always staying over at one place or another, so everyone knows their name. Hints Kyaku looks just like any other customer. Picture a stereotypical "customer" type person in your head.

meaningMnemonic: The heavy radical and the heavy kanji are the same. Hints Know your radicals, yo!
readingMnemonic: In your hand is a very heavy jew el ( じゅう ). Real jewels are always heavier than they look. Hints Imagine holding a real jewel in your right hand and a fake jewel in your left. The one in your right hand is suuuuupeerrr heavy!

meaningMnemonic: You dig under a cliff to find two tree s and a stop sign. These things must have a history ! Try to imagine what history these two trees and a stop sign reveal to you, here under this cliff. Hints Imagine touching the dead tree bark, the rusted stop sign. Their history stretches back to ancient times — when trees still grew on Earth, and people needed stop signs because they didn't have self-driving air-taxis. How fascinating.
readingMnemonic: To really dig up more history like this, you need a wrecki ng ( れき ) ball. Luckily you've brought one, so you get to work smashing the cliff apart to overturn as much history you can, with your wrecking ball. Hints Hear the cliff crack and splinter from the force of the wrecking ball. That's the sound of history being revealed.

meaningMnemonic: The history radical and the history kanji are the same. Hints Radicals have a history of sometimes reappearing as kanji later on, don't they?
readingMnemonic: History was full of famous shee p ( し ). Sure, there were important people in history too, but historical sheep are where it's at. Hints Imagine reading about sheep in a history book. There's Dolly, the first sheep clone in history, for example. And then there's… well, I'm sure there are tons.

meaningMnemonic: You need to get your fingers around a temple if you want to hold it. Is the temple too big? Hold smaller temples you can buy in the temple's souvenir shop. Hints Imagine holding a tiny temple in your fingers. Hold it up to the light. Hold it on the train. Hold it while you sleep.
readingMnemonic: As you hold the temple you hear a voice. You look down through your fingers and see a tiny Je sus ( じ ). He's smiling and gives you a thumbs up. Aww, thanks Jesus! Hints Jesus likes when you hold things like temples. He probably likes when you hold other things too, like ice cream, puppies, and homeless peoples' hands.

meaningMnemonic: The leader of the elephant s is so great, they put up an image or statue of him everywhere. Every house, every street corner — his image looks down on all the other elephants at all times. Hints For now, just imagine the leader of the elephants being told images and statues of him are being put up everywhere. Don't think about what the statue looks like, because that's next.
readingMnemonic: When they unveil the image s and statue s of the leader elephant, everyone gasps. They look like him, but he's a zo mbie ( ぞう ). Gasp! Hints But this is exactly what the leader of the elephants asked for. You see, the leader of the elephants was a big fan of zombies. Imagine how excited he'd get to have this zombie version of himself appearing as images and statues, all across the land.

meaningMnemonic: When you're in prison , whoever ends up with the shellfish will lose . It's the game all prisoners play. It's like keep away from the shellfish. And if you end up with the shellfish BZZZZTT that's it, you're the loser. Hints Imagine that it's your first day in prison. You're walking around the yard, minding your own business, when suddenly a shellfish smacks you right in the head and falls into your open hands. "HAHA YOU LOSE!" someone shouts.
readingMnemonic: If you lose , you're a foo l ( ふ ). All you had to do was not hold the prison shellfish. It really shouldn't have been that hard to not lose, ya fool. Hints Now you have to try to make some other fool lose. Otherwise you'll be the loser fool forever.

meaningMnemonic: You need to look a tree in the eye to gain a mutual respect for each other. Stand up straight, look the tree directly in its eye(s). If it looks right back, you know things are mutual. Hints It's the same with humans, you know? If you want to have a mutual relationship you need to be able to look each other in the eyes. If you're too embarrassed, or you look down on them, then that isn't mutual respect!
readingMnemonic: If your respect for the tree is mutual with the respect the tree feels for you, you'll be able to see the tree's sou l ( そう ). Right now its soul looks pretty sad, like it's trying to say, "Why are your people cutting down all my friends? I thought we had a mutual understanding." Hints This is basically a FernGully moment, you know? You can feel the tree's pain like it's your pain. It's that kind of mutual sharing of souls you need.

meaningMnemonic: When a helicopter is piloted by a woman , it stirs an insatiable need in her. She doesn't know what it is. But she needs it. And that's why she's flying around looking for it! Hints Picture the woman in the helicopter needing something. She's looking around. Searching. But she doesn't know what it is!
readingMnemonic: Finally she knows what she need s! It's yo gurt ( よう )! Delicious, creamy yogurt! Hints What does she need? Yogurt!

meaningMnemonic: There's a stand ing tree that you're taking an axe to. You're going to cut down this tree to let a new tree grow. Hints As you imagine yourself cutting down the standing tree, think about what new tree you'll plant in its place.
readingMnemonic: You cut down the tree to make room for a new one, but it falls on your shin ( しん ). Hints Only your shin got hit, so focus all your imaginary pain down there. Try to pull out the splinters. Ouch!

meaningMnemonic: You find a cross in the mouth of Wolverine . What a strange occurrence . I guess he put it there, but why would he do such a thing ? You ask him, but he says it's a personal matter of utmost secrecy. Hints Imagine his muffled words as he tries to explain this with the cross in his mouth. Hm, better not pry further. Maybe he's trying to… X-orcize his demons…
readingMnemonic: This occurrence doesn't impress Je sus ( じ ), who appears and gently removes the cross from Wolverine's mouth. Hints Imagine Jesus gently taking the cross out of Wolverine's mouth. What a swell dude.

meaningMnemonic: The clown building is over in that part of town. We keep the clown part as separate as we can from the rest of the normal people. In fact, the entire clown education department and their clown club s have to stay in their part, they can't come in ours. Hints Of course, we feel terrible about forcing the clowns into their own part of town. It's not that they're lesser than us, it's just that we don't like them.
readingMnemonic: You see, that part of town is full of boo ze ( ぶ ). Clowns need a lot of booze to keep their charade going, so we just let them have it. But they aren't allowed in our part anymore, because they all stink of nasty clown booze. Hints Picture all of the clowns, trapped in their weird clown part of town, drinking booze and smashing each other over the heads with the bottles. You're glad you don't live in that part.

meaningMnemonic: When everyone has grain in their mouth , you will have peace . That is the Japanese style of doing things. Hints Imagine Japanese people with grain in their mouth. The whole country is at peace.
readingMnemonic: Peace is the Japanese style . The wa lruses ( わ ) living off of Japan see this, and start to emulate. Hints The walruses also achieve peace by putting grain in every walrus' mouth, following the Japanese style.

meaningMnemonic: The eye of a lion , still small and curious, gazes upon the prefecture that will one day become his. He's a small lion, but once he grows up, everything reflected in his eye will be his prefecture to rule over. Hints Imagine the small lion casting his eye across his future prefecture. His small eye is twinkling, because he's proud that he'll one day be prefect, and this prefecture will be his.
readingMnemonic: This small lion's prefecture is being protected by Ken ( けん ) the samurai, because the lion is too small to protect all of this land himself. Ken the samurai is used to wandering far and wide, so one prefecture is nothing to him. Hints Picture Ken protecting the prefecture, punching hyenas in the face, and yelling, "This may just be a prefecture, not a country, but I'll give it my all for my lion prefect-to-be!"

meaningMnemonic: The mouth of a tree leader is all about trying to preserve the trees. In fact, she guarantee s that she will preserve the trees if it's the last thing she does. Hints Basically, a tree leader is someone who stands up for trees. Mostly she talks, but that can be a powerful skill to have.
readingMnemonic: She chains herself to a tree to preserve them. But, unfortunately, the lumberjacks just take a giant back hoe ( ほ ) and tear this tree leader and the tree she's attached to in half. Hints What a terrible scene. Focus on the fact that they're using a horrible, modified back hoe. It's more like a weapon than a back hoe, and they show no mercy at all.

meaningMnemonic: Your scooter is anti scoot. It doesn't want to run. So you have to return it. Hints Unfortunately, now you have to return to the store to return this scooter, but you have no scooter to get there with. Ugh.
readingMnemonic: You return to the store and wait in line to return the scooter but the person working returns doesn't want you to return it. He stares you dead in the eyes, waves his hand, and turns you into a hen ( へん )! Hints The employee leans down toward you in hen form and says, "Ooh, I'm sorry. We don't take returns from hens. You'll have to just return home."

meaningMnemonic: You put a grain in your mouth and let it take a ride . This kanji has the same radicals as 和 , but this time the grain is in your mouth, which is why there's little pieces of grain sticking out of the 口 part ;) Hints Just imagine you're a car or a train and the grain is a person. It's going for a nice ride in your mouth!
readingMnemonic: You decide the grain is probably lonely on this ride alone, so you add some no ri ( の ) seaweed, so it has a friend. Hints Now the nori is going for a ride too, woohoo!

meaningMnemonic: You plant a flag in the ground , marking your private patch of dirt . In this spot you raise a roof , then fill the space beneath it with some shop s and store s. Hints That's the natural next progression of claiming some land. Building a roof upon it and building some shops and stores inside. You'll see why in a moment.
readingMnemonic: The roof covering the dirt is there so that the Ya nkees ( や ) can play baseball year round. The store s and shop s are there to sell hot dogs and Yankees memorabilia. Hints You have yourself a whole Yankees stadium, and all it took was a roof and some shops and stores! If you build it, they will come.

meaningMnemonic: A samurai has come bearing forehead s and legs that he's trying to sell . He thought it was a waste to leave all his slain enemies on the battlefield, so he gathered up their foreheads and legs to sell on the black market for some extra cash. Hey, no judging! A samurai's gotta sell what a samurai's gotta sell, okay? Hints Imagine running into this samurai salesman as you walk through a sketchy part of town. He cautiously glances over his shoulder before opening his trench coat to reveal to you… all the foreheads and legs he's trying to sell.
readingMnemonic: If you run into this samurai who sell s severed foreheads and legs, you should just say " bye ( ばい )!" and get the heck out of there. Actually, if anyone tries to sell you severed body parts — samurai or not — you should probably say bye over and over until you can get away from them. Hints Imagine loudly saying "bye" over and over at this shady samurai. He keeps trying to tell you about how fresh and high-quality all his foreheads and legs are, but you just loudly repeat "bye" as you back away from him.

meaningMnemonic: On its scooter , a creature with horns from heaven will take things you want to send there. Hints Picture the horned thing on its scooter, a big messenger bag over its shoulder with the kanji for heaven on it. "You got somethin' you want me to send?" it mutters.
readingMnemonic: You want to send your sou l ( そう ) to heaven. I mean, you don't want it to go to some of those other places you've heard of, so why not send your soul? Hints You put your soul into an envelope, stick a stamp on it, and hand it off to be sent to heaven. Bye-bye! I hope this doesn't have any negative effects on your body!

meaningMnemonic: The spicy radical and spicy kanji are exactly the same! Hot!
readingMnemonic: When you eat spicy food, it gives a から て chop to your mouth. That's where that spicy feeling comes from! Hints Imagine a bunch of little black belt spice molecules からて punching, kicking and chopping all the way through your mouth and into your throat and nasal passages. Oww, it's pure agony!

meaningMnemonic: The flowers have grown old , so they're suffering . Hints Flowers, like anything that grows old, go through a lot of suffering as their bodies break down. They're no different from you and me.
readingMnemonic: If a flower or a person is growing old and suffering , give them a coo kie ( く ). Hints No one can resist a good cookie. It will ease your suffering, or at least distract you for a little bit.

meaningMnemonic: If a tsunami is going to last an eternity you better learn how to swim now. We'll be under water for the rest of time and if you can't swim you're not gonna make it. Hints Picture most of the earth's population already swimming on the tsunami that will last the rest of eternity. Your floaties and life preservers would help you through this mess. You need to swim!
readingMnemonic: Oy ( およ )! Oy, stop daydreaming about swim ming and actually do it! Hints Picture yourself swimming in the tsunami with everyone else. You can't really talk to them, you're too busy swimming for your life, so you just shout "Oy!" to them and they shout it back.

meaningMnemonic: You say things around a fire . In fact there are two fire s, and you're talk ing with a group of people, all sitting around two nice campfires. Hints Imagine yourself next to the two campfires, having a heart-to-heart talk. What are you saying?
readingMnemonic: You talk in this intense, fiery way all the way until dawn ( だん ), but no longer! Once dawn comes the discussion needs to be concluded. Hints If you try to talk all night and past dawn, you'll burn out. Take the day, think, then tonight you can try to have an all-night talk again.

meaningMnemonic: Your leader is very anti -everything, making it all temporary . You get a new shirt, "I'm anti shirts!" she yells, and out it goes. Hints She tires of things so quickly, you hardly have time to get used to them before they're gone.
readingMnemonic: The leader's most temporary possession is her ca r ( か ). Or... cars, because they're all very temporary. She buys one, drives it around, and then suddenly she's anti red car. She needs a blue one! Hints Picture all of the temporary cars she's tried filling up an entire junkyard. They're all a little different, but in the end they were all just temporary fads.

meaningMnemonic: A horse and a squid are going to test you. Hints Imagine the horse and squid in a big testing room, getting ready to test you. What are they testing you on? Weirdly, they're going to test you on all the kanji that use horse and squid radicals. You ready?
readingMnemonic: The test is being supervised by Ken ( けん ) the samurai. Hints To make sure you don't cheat on the horse and the squid test, Ken the samurai is watching you closely, pacing up and down. Every now and then, he waves his katana menacingly.

meaningMnemonic: A cow with wing s is flying in the air. What a strange thing ! You've heard of flying pigs before, but cows? This is a new and strange thing indeed! Cows with wings! What a silly thing. Hints Imagine if cows could fly. Wouldn't you be jealous of them? I mean, if a cow can fly, any old thing should be able to, right?
readingMnemonic: You want a thing to help you fly with the cow so you put on your flying boots ( ぶつ ). Your flying boots are a pretty strange thing in themselves, but they're the only way you can keep up. Hints Imagine a thing like flying boots. Do you believe such a thing could be real?

meaningMnemonic: There's an eye on the ground , among some fins . What happened? You killed a fish, and now you must hide the murder tool . Quick, hide the tool before someone finds out it was you. Hints You feel the panic upon realizing what you've just done. This is murder in the first degree. You used a terrible tool to do it, and now you must hide it.
readingMnemonic: The tool is dripping with goo ( ぐ ). Goopy, incriminating goo. It's the guts of the fish you just killed and it's all over your hands too. Yuck. Hints That goo is really slimy. It's disgusting. You feel sick to your stomach. Please don't throw up, there's already enough junk on the ground with the eye and fins and all.

meaningMnemonic: Go up on the roof in spring to see the truth . The reality of the world is being revealed as winter ends and the trees bear fruit once again. Hints Imagine sitting comfortably on your roof as everything around you changes to spring. Snow melts and reveals the truth of all the trees and plants it was hiding, which now begin to bear fruit.
readingMnemonic: As the snow melts and reveals the truth and reality of the world to you, you notice one of the trees you were looking at has already borne two piece of fruit . Gee, two ( じつ )?! That's a lot of fruit for this early in the spring. Hints Imagine examining the fruits as you say, "Gee, two?" over and over again in disbelief. It's the truth, though. No matter how many times you say "gee, two?" the reality of the situation will not change.

meaningMnemonic: If you want to say something at a ceremony for construction workers you're going to have to try really hard. Construction is loud, so if you want to be heard you have to attempt to be louder than the drilling and smashing and digging and handing out of awards. Hints Try to imagine trying this hard to be heard. The construction workers are all screaming at each other with ease. It's so hard for you to try and keep up with their volume!
readingMnemonic: You try to get their attention the only way you know how, by lifting a shee p ( し ) above your head. The sheep baas and suddenly everything is silent, all eyes are on you. Well, they're on the sheep. Hints Huh. You should have thought to try this sheep technique earlier.

meaningMnemonic: The moon grants a gladiator its power so he will win ! Victory will be his! Hints Watch as the moon's power fills the gladiator. He starts to glow, grows larger, and has some craters on his face now. Well.. okay.
readingMnemonic: He win s over and over again, and soon the Shou gun ( しょう ) is even rooting for him. In fact, the Shougun claims him as his personal gladiator of choice. Hints The Shougun is only interested in people who win. But you probably could have guessed that already.

meaningMnemonic: Every rice paddy sits jammed in to the world . Hints The world is basically just a bunch of rice paddies smooshed together, if you think about it.
readingMnemonic: To get around this world of rice paddies, you need to use a kay ak ( かい ). Hints A rice paddy is mostly made up of water, just like our world, and you don't want to have wet feet. Use the power of your kayak to become a world traveler.

meaningMnemonic: If you take all part s and put them together, you have all things. The entire collection. It is whole .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: リンゴを全部買うつもりです。
sentences.english: I'm going to buy all the apples.

sentences.japanese: 全部の科目のテストで良いスコアでした。
sentences.english: I got good test scores in all subjects.

sentences.japanese: 私のベーコンクッキー全部食べたのは一体だれ！？
sentences.english: Who the hell ate all my bacon cookies?!

meaningMnemonic: An angle degree is just an angle . 90 degrees? 160 degrees? They're all still angles when you come down to it.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 正しい角度にするのに時間がかかりました。
sentences.english: It took a while to get the angle right.

sentences.japanese: これについては、色々な角度から見て考えてみたいと思います。
sentences.english: I would like to think about this from various angles.

sentences.japanese: 一つの角度が全て六十度ということは、それは「正三角形」ですよ。
sentences.english: Each angle is sixty degrees, which means it's an "equilateral triangle."

meaningMnemonic: I'm going to express my departure . That is my only announcement .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The ひょう changes to ぴょう and the はつ gets shortened, though, so just about everything about this word is weird.

sentences.japanese: それでは、発表します。スピーチコンテストの勝者は田中さんです！
sentences.english: Now for the announcement. The winner of the speech contest is Mr. Tanaka!

sentences.japanese: 大学のプレゼンテーション発表会に参加しました。
sentences.english: I participated in the university presentation conference.

sentences.japanese: 社長が会社とスタッフにとって、とても大切な発表をしたいそうです。
sentences.english: Apparently, the president wants to make a very important announcement for the company and the staff.

meaningMnemonic: When you write down a lot of stuff focusing on one thing it's called an article . If it's on something that just happened it will probably be a news story .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: この記事の作者は、アメリカ人ジャーナリストです。
sentences.english: The author of this article is an American journalist.

sentences.japanese: 外交についての記事があまりない。
sentences.english: There are not many articles about diplomacy.

sentences.japanese: 今月号の記事はデタラメばっかりだよ。
sentences.english: The articles from this month's issue are full of nonsense.

meaningMnemonic: A temporary determination is something you're not totally sure about. You've decided to think of something in a certain way, but only for now. If more information comes to light, you may change your mind. That's why this word means assumption . 仮定 refers to making tentative assumptions about a specific situation to discuss what might happen under certain conditions, such as "if we assume I dropped my wallet here yesterday...”
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: それは、仮定ではなく、本当のことです。
sentences.english: It is not a assumption, but the truth.

sentences.japanese: たとえば、一ドル百円と仮定すると、一本一ドルのコカコーラは百円になりますよね？
sentences.english: For example, if we say one dollar is one hundred yen, then one can of $1 coca cola is one hundred yen, right?

sentences.japanese: 仮定を立てる前に、もう一回しっかりと仮定を立てる理由を考えましょう。
sentences.english: Before making a hypothesis, really think again about your reasons for making it.

meaningMnemonic: You know the word 通る hopefully by now. That is the verb version of this word, which means "to pass through." So, if this is the noun version, what is it that you use to pass through something? To drive or walk along? That would be an avenue (or street , road , etc). This is a pretty common word in Japan, and good for not getting lost.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the word 通る , so as long as you know that, you should be able to read this one as well. Mind the strange long お sound!

sentences.english: to go out on the street

sentences.japanese: この通りを右に行って下さい。
sentences.english: Go to the right on this street.

sentences.japanese: 下町の通りには、たくさんのお店が有って、一日中、人々が行ったり来たりします。
sentences.english: Streets in the Shitamachi area have lots of shops, and people come and go throughout the day.

sentences.japanese: 東京には、「竹下通り」という名の通りがあって、中学生や高校生に人気です。
sentences.english: There is a street called "Takeshita Street" in Tokyo, which is popular with junior high and high school students.

meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. More precisely, it has しい on the end, which makes it even more likely it's an adjective. What's the adjective form of beauty ? It's beautiful .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you. It's a long reading for a mnemonic, but try your best. You look at someone who is beautiful . What an easy life they've lived. No hard work and all they do is pamper themselves to stay beautiful. Feel disgusted. You walk up to this person and say: " U too cushy ! ( うつくしい ). Sorry for adding the whole word in there for the reading mnemonic, but I thought it worked out better that way. Just know that the word isn't うつくしいしい or something weird like that. The hiragana on the end is part of the mnemonic as well.

sentences.japanese: コントラストが美しい
この青い花、とても美しいですね。
sentences.english: This blue flower is very beautiful.

sentences.japanese: 四国の「四万十川」という名の川は日本の美しい川の一つです。
sentences.english: The river called "Shimanto River" in Shikoku is one of Japan's beautiful rivers.

sentences.japanese: この人形の目は、宝石のように美しいですね。
sentences.english: The eyes of this doll are beautiful like jewels.

meaningMnemonic: A beautiful person is a beautiful woman . Wait, why isn't this a beautiful person? In fact, this word used to have a broader meaning, but for some reason it's generally only used for women in modern Japanese.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: Where you're from, every beautiful woman wears bee jean s ( びじん ). That's right, jeans made out of bees. Beauty knows no pain after all!

sentences.japanese: あの女の人は、とてもエレガントな美人ですね。
sentences.english: That woman is a very elegant beauty.

sentences.japanese: 電話番号をきく時、「あなた美人ですね」ってどうしても言えなかったんだよ。
sentences.english: When I asked for her phone number, I just couldn't say, "You're a beautiful woman."

sentences.japanese: あいつ、「だれの助言もいらない」って言ってたのに、美人の助言はウェルカムなんだとよ。
sentences.english: He said, "I don't need anyone's advice," but then he said he would welcome advice from beautiful women.

meaningMnemonic: You take your 気 (energy) and 付ける (attach) it to whatever you're doing, allowing you to focus in and be careful . Since this word is in the te-form, it's a soft imperative. You're basically telling someone, "hey, take care , okay?" 気を付けて is an everyday expression used a lot when telling someone to watch out, stay safe, or be mindful of something. Note that 気をつけて without the kanji 付 is also common, especially in casual writing.
readingMnemonic: The readings come from the two words 気 and 付ける . So long as you know those from the previous levels, you should be able to read this one as well.

sentences.japanese: ストーブの火に気を付けて下さい。
sentences.english: Please be careful of the fire in the heater.

sentences.japanese: 今日は雨かもしれないから、外出する時は気を付けてレインコートをもってね。
sentences.english: It might rain today, so be careful and take a raincoat when you go out.

sentences.japanese: この国の大きな町では、スリが多いから気を付けてね。
sentences.english: Be careful in big cities in this country, because there are many pickpockets.

sentences.japanese: 辺りは明るくないので、足元に気を付けて下さい。
sentences.english: There's not much light around here, so watch your feet.

meaningMnemonic: Something is both white and black . It is black and white (you can also say white and black if you prefer).
readingMnemonic: The readings are kun'yomi, but you should have seen both 白 and 黒い separately as vocabulary by now. It's the same readings here, so you can apply that knowledge and read this word!

sentences.japanese: 七十年前、テレビは白黒でした。
sentences.english: Seventy years ago, TV was black and white.

sentences.japanese: 白黒ハッキリつけようぜ。
sentences.english: Let’s put it in very black and white terms.

sentences.japanese: カナエちゃん、今日の全身白黒の服は、ちょっとパンダみたいじゃない？
sentences.english: Kanae-chan, don't you look a bit like a panda in your black and white outfit today?

meaningMnemonic: How heavy is your body ? Figure that out and you'll have your body weight .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 体重をコントロールする

sentences.english: to be over a weight limit
to not have enough body weight

sentences.japanese: アンナさんの体重は、何キロですか？
sentences.english: What is Anna’s body weight in kilograms?

sentences.japanese: うちの犬は去年太ったが、必死のダイエットで一気に体重が下がりました。
sentences.english: Our dog ​​got fat last year, but she lost the weight all at once on a desperate diet.

sentences.japanese: すみません。この体重、コンタクトレンズの分も入ってますよね？
sentences.english: Excuse me. This weight takes my contact lenses into account too, right?

meaningMnemonic: A book shop is a shop that sells books. A bookstore .
readingMnemonic: The readings are the ones that you learned with the kanji.

sentences.japanese: 先日、友人と本屋に行きました。
sentences.english: The other day, I went to the bookstore with a friend.

sentences.japanese: 三日前、本屋で有名な作家の本を買いました。
sentences.english: Three days ago, I bought a book by a famous writer at the bookstore.

sentences.japanese: 私は新しい本を買うために、前の日から本屋の前でキャンプをしました。
sentences.english: I camped out in front of the bookstore a day early in order to buy a new book.

meaningMnemonic: A meat shop is a place that sells meat. Who sells meat? A butcher shop ! 肉屋 often refers to the butcher shop, but it can also mean the actual butchers who work there. You might also see this as お肉屋さん , but that won't change the meaning — it can still be either the shop or the butcher, depending on context!
readingMnemonic: For 肉 you use the にく reading (which you learned with the kanji). For 屋 you use the kun'yomi, which you learned with the kanji. Basically, if you learned the kanji readings, you can read this word!

sentences.english: to work at the butcher shop
to buy at the butcher shop
to receive at the butcher shop
in front of the butcher shop

sentences.japanese: 肉屋さんで牛肉を四百グラム買いました。
sentences.english: I bought 400 grams of beef at the butcher shop.

sentences.japanese: 日本の肉屋さんでは、コロッケやカツなどが売ってますよ。
sentences.english: Japanese butchers sell croquettes and cutlets.

sentences.japanese: 私の生まれた小さい町には「お肉屋さん」と言う名前のベジタリアンのレストランがあったの。今思い出すと、なんだか皮肉な名前よね。
sentences.english: In the small town where I was born, there was a vegetarian restaurant named "Butcher." Now that I recall it, it's kind of a sarcastic name.

meaningMnemonic: If you mix and substitute two people, that's a change of personnel, or a substitution . Perhaps those people are even working in shift s, so they mix and substitute each other at regular intervals. You'll see this word in pretty diverse contexts, because it can refer to anything from a change of political regime, to the substitution of a player during a match, to factory shifts. The underlying meaning is that one person or group is switched out with another.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 代 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you: A change calls for a tie ( たい ). If you're the new company president, or you're going in to work to start your shift, you'd better make sure you look the part, so get that tie nice and straight.

sentences.english: to go in as a substitute

sentences.japanese: ラグビーなど、多くのスポーツで交代のルールがあります。
sentences.english: In many sports, such as rugby, there are rules for substitution.

sentences.japanese: 父と母は毎日交代で夜ごはんを作ります。
sentences.english: My father and mother take turns making dinner every day.

sentences.japanese: 先日、十六年ぶりに社長交代がありました。
sentences.english: The other day, there was a change of company president for the first time in sixteen years.

sentences.japanese: そろそろ交代してもらえませんか？
sentences.english: Could you switch in for me soon?

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the reading you learned with the kanji and uses the on'yomi even though it's a single word. Very strange, but convenient for you so long as you remember this exception reading word.

sentences.japanese: うちの母は、ラッキーカラーが赤なので、いつも赤い服をきています。
sentences.english: My mother's lucky color is red, so she always wears red clothes.

sentences.japanese: どれだけ持っていても服が足りないのは、なぜ？！
sentences.english: Why is it that I never have enough clothes no matter how many I own?!

sentences.japanese: 服を全部引き出しの中に入れてください。
sentences.english: Put all the clothes in the drawer.

meaningMnemonic: Construction occurrences are just different kinds of construction ! 工事 often refers to construction work , especially for buildings, roads, and other infrastructure projects. But it can also cover repairs, upgrades, and installations of things like electrical systems, plumbing, phone lines, and internet as well.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 工事は今日から明日までです。
sentences.english: The construction is from today to tomorrow.

sentences.japanese: この道は今工事中なので、左に行って下さい。
sentences.english: This road is under construction now, so please take a left.

sentences.japanese: 夕べは工事の音がうるさくて、ねむれませんでした。
sentences.english: I couldn't sleep because of the noise of the construction last night.

meaningMnemonic: A mutual talk . Both sides are talking to each other and the feelings are mutual. Imagine you're discussing a problem. You want to get help with it, so you get some consultation from your friend. This discussion was very helpful.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: ねえ、相談があるんだけど。
sentences.english: Hey, I have something I want to discuss with you.

sentences.japanese: 家のローン相談は、午後六時から午後九時です。
sentences.english: Home loan consultation is from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m.

sentences.japanese: 医者に相談したら「先ずはストレスのない生活をして下さい」と言われました。
sentences.english: When I consulted the doctor, I was told, "First, try to live a life without stress."

meaningMnemonic: When you look at something versus something else, you compare them with one another. You look at the contrast between them and make a comparison .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 日本の生活とアメリカの生活じゃ、いい対比にならないよ。
sentences.english: Japanese life and American life don't make for a good comparison.

sentences.japanese: では、この魚とその魚を対比してみましょう。
sentences.english: Now let's compare this fish with that one.

sentences.japanese: 日本とアメリカの映画のポスターを対比してみました。
sentences.english: I compared Japanese and American movie posters.

meaningMnemonic: Alright, so this one's a bit weird. See that oddly small ヶ there? Well, together with 月 ( month ), it becomes a counter for months . You'll use this when you want to talk about a specific number of months, so not when you're saying January, February, etc. Note that you'll run into different variants of this. While 一ヶ月 is the most common, you'll also encounter 一か月 , 一カ月 , and rarely 一箇月 . Luckily, they're all read the same, just written differently. Speaking about reading, let's get to it.
readingMnemonic: The little ヶ might be slightly misleading, as you'll have to read this as か . The rest is easy though, as 月 just takes a normal on'yomi reading. And since we're not talking about specific months, that means it's just げつ , making this 〜かげつ .

sentences.japanese: 日本の学校の夏休みは一ヶ月しかありません。
sentences.english: Japanese schools only have one month of summer vacation.

sentences.japanese: これが出来上がるまでに数ヶ月かかりました。
sentences.english: It took several months to complete this.

sentences.japanese: 赤ちゃん、今何ヶ月ですか？
sentences.english: How many months old is the baby?

sentences.japanese: うちの子は八ヶ月でハイハイをして、九ヶ月で歩き出しました。
sentences.english: My child started crawling at eight months and began walking at nine months.

meaningMnemonic: It's been decide d and determine d. The decision has been made.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just be sure to take note of the shortened けつ in 決 . It goes to けっ .

sentences.japanese: 今すぐは決定出来ません。
アメリカに支店をオープンするかどうかは明日のミーティングで決定します。
sentences.english: We'll decide in tomorrow's meeting whether to open a branch in the United States.

sentences.japanese: ホリコシ先生、ご自分のマンガのアニメ化決定について、どう思われますか？
sentences.english: Horikoshi-sensei, how do you feel about the decision to animate your manga?

meaningMnemonic: The kanji degree can mean both degree in terms of angles and degree in terms of temperature. This word is how you talk about these things. Just attach it to a number and you have yourself the number of degrees that something is. After the numbers 1, 2 and 3 (and in some other situations) this can also mean times .
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the kanji reading you learned. When writing out the answer to this reading, omit the 〜 as it's only there to let you know that some other word should come before it.

sentences.japanese: 東京の夏は、三十度以上になる日が多いです。
sentences.english: In Tokyo in summer, there are many days where it gets above thirty degrees.

sentences.japanese: 先ず、オーブンを１９０度にして下さい。
sentences.english: First, heat the oven to 190 degrees.
The angle here is ninety degrees.

meaningMnemonic: You exit and then make a departure . This is just a departure .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The しゅつ gets shortened and はつ changes to ぱつ . No wonder you want to make a departure, you want to get away from crazy readings like this.

sentences.english: to inform someone of a departure
There are five minutes until departure.

sentences.japanese: 二週間後に、東京に出発する予定です。
sentences.english: I'm going to leave for Tokyo in two weeks.

sentences.japanese: フェリーが出発するまでの時間、お茶でものみましょうよ。
sentences.english: Let's have some tea until the ferry departs.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how 自由 means freedom? Well when you add not it causes you discomfort and really inconveniences you. That not is in the way of your freedom.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.english: to seem impaired, to seem inconvenienced
to look inconvenient, to look disabled

sentences.japanese: 母は足が不自由なので、車をつかうことが多いです。
sentences.english: My mother has a leg disability, so she often uses a car.

sentences.japanese: ここは、おじいちゃん・おばあちゃん、体の不自由な方のためのベンチです。
sentences.english: This is a bench for grandpas, grandmas, and people with physical disabilities.

sentences.japanese: 不自由な生活を送っている人々をサポートするために、国民全員が助力するべきです。
sentences.english: Every citizen should help out to support those who live life with disabilities.

meaningMnemonic: You make departure from your home off into the great beyond. You will go to see the unseen, and hopefully make a great discovery .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You know the はつ part, which gets shortened to はっ . The 見 is unlike what you learned with 見 , though. In order to remember that this is けん , imagine you're going out to make a discovery of some strange new lands. With strange new lands, there comes strange new people. This one has a samurai named Ken ( けん ) on it. He's trying to discover new things too!

sentences.english: to be able to make a discovery

sentences.japanese: 木の上に毛虫を発見しました。
sentences.english: I found a caterpillar on a tree.

sentences.japanese: 外国で生活をしていると、毎日発見があります。
sentences.english: If you live in a foreign country, you'll make discoveries every day.

sentences.japanese: この古い地図があれば、宝を発見することが出来るかもしれない。
sentences.english: With this old map, you may be able to find some treasure.

meaningMnemonic: When you have two heavy things, you have double and dual the heavy (compared to one, at least). This word is a prefix attached to other words to show that it is "double." 二重 kanji time!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 分からない文字の下に、二重のラインを引いて下さい。
sentences.english: Please draw a double line under characters you're not sure about.

sentences.japanese: この魚はニオイが強いので、ラップを二重にしておきますね。
sentences.english: This fish has a strong smell, so I'll double wrap it.

sentences.japanese: これは、二重アゴをなくすためのエクササイズです。
sentences.english: This is an exercise to get rid of double chins.

meaningMnemonic: When something happens at every occurrence and at every degree , it's something that happens frequently . It happens each time .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 毎度ありがとうございます
sentences.english: thank you for your continued patronage
thank you for your continued patronage (short for 毎度ありがとうございます)

sentences.japanese: 毎度、同じエラーが出るんですよ。
sentences.english: Every time, I get the same error.

sentences.japanese: もちろんクソリプは毎度スルーだよ。
sentences.english: Of course, I always ignore hateful replies.

sentences.japanese: 毎度のことだが、キョーコは今日も服を決めるのに時間がかかっている。
sentences.english: This always happens, but it’s taking a long time for Kyoko to decide on what to wear today too.

meaningMnemonic: A win that was an ease . That is an easy victory or an easy win . Don't hope for a lot of these, though. Hope for tough wins instead, they actually make you better. Note that this can be used both literally, to describe an easy victory at a game or contest; or more figuratively, to describe something as “easy” in general.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 今回のテストは、楽勝だったね。
sentences.english: This test was a piece of cake.

sentences.japanese: 「JLPT5はどうだった？」「ワニカニのおかげで、楽勝だったよ。」
sentences.english: ”How was the JLPT5?" "Thanks to WaniKani, it was easy peasy."

sentences.japanese: あのゲームは楽勝すぎて、なんかつまらないんだよね。
sentences.english: That game is such a piece of cake that it's just kinda boring.

meaningMnemonic: You've seen 学校 from a couple levels ago. Now we're adding a small to it. What is a "small school"? That's a school for small people, making it an elementary school .
readingMnemonic: The reading is the regular on'yomi reading of 小 plus the vocab word 学校 that you've seen previously. Combine these two things for the reading of 小学校 .

sentences.english: to be admitted to an elementary school, to enroll in an elementary school
to enter elementary school, to get into elementary school
in front of the elementary school
elementary school admission, elementary school enrollment

sentences.japanese: 私は小学校の先生です。
sentences.english: I am an elementary school teacher.

sentences.japanese: この町の小学校には、外国生まれの生徒もたくさんいますよ。
sentences.english: There are many foreign-born students in the elementary school in this town.

sentences.japanese: 小学校の子どもたちに、絵本をよむボランティアの会に入ってます。
sentences.english: I am in a volunteer club that reads picture books to elementary school children.

sentences.japanese: 小学校の時から、君のこと、ずっと気になっていたんだ。
sentences.english: I've been interested in you since we were in elementary school.

meaningMnemonic: When something has a heavy need , you know that that thing is essential . It is important .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: Now, I'd like to try an experiment to see what I have to say to get my mother to give me money.

sentences.japanese: 父は事実、それを知っていました。

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

meaningMnemonic: Go ahead and try an eat . How was that little try? That little food sample ? That little taste ? sentences.english: It's almost like I'm going to Costco to eat the food samples.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

meaningMnemonic: Your house tools aren't the tools you use to build a house. They're more like the things that are a part of your house that you use like tools. Those things would be your furniture . So, remember, your house tools are just furniture.

Car furniture is such a flex.

meaningMnemonic: The さん on the end is the name honorific さん . It's there to show some respect. It's like saying "Mr. Guest!" or something like that. But that sounds dumb in English. We'll just call this word guest , visitor , or customer . You'll hear this word a lot when you're at a store or you're a customer somewhere in Japan. You are the お客さん , in that situation. Alternatively, you'll also hear お客さま which is a more polite version of this word (because it ends in さま and not さん ).
readingMnemonic: The reading is the reading you learned with the kanji. Just add the hiragana on the end and you'll be good to go.

sentences.english: My grandmother is good at making heart-shaped rice balls.

meaningMnemonic: You know 事 means "occurrence," but it can also mean "matter." And if something is a big matter to someone, it must be a very important and valuable thing to them. 大事 describes something that holds great importance or value. For example, you can use 大事 to describe something or someone that matters a lot to you. You can also use 大事 to describe a crucial task or moment. And if you want to bring up a serious topic, you may say that you have something 大事 to talk about.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 大 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: Nothing in your life is as important or valuable to you as dye s ( だい ). You really just love dyes more than anything else. Dyes, dyes, dyes!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

meaningMnemonic: The temporary name s. These are the kana (that's hiragana and katakana). Why are kana the "temporary names" though? Maybe they were just meant to be a temporary way to write the names of the kanji you didn't know how to write yet. That's just a guess, but it should help you remember that this word means "kana."
readingMnemonic: Okay, so 仮 uses the rare kun'yomi reading か , which you haven't learned yet, but luckily it's the same as the on'yomi you have learned! And 名 also uses a kun'yomi reading that you learned with the vocab word 名 ( な ). So you sort of know these readings already, but it's a lot to take in, so here's a mnemonic to help: The reading is so tricky for kana that it makes you say かな … (I wonder…) whenever you try to read it. You keep thinking, "Is the reading kana, かな ? Or could it be something else, かな ?" You're just not sure.

readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi of both kanji, and you haven't learned this kun'yomi for 空 yet. As long as you know the meaning, the reading should be easy, but here's a mnemonic to help you just in case: Karate comes from ( から ) Japan!

meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of new ? It's new .

This is an Atara ... a knockoff video game system :(

sentences.english: the way of thinking is new

the beginning of the new year

You're so full of yourself (even in front of the sea/ocean) that you reply: " um, me ?" ( うみ ). Imagine yourself feeling this full of yourself.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how words beginning with あ show that whatever you're talking about is far away from both you and the person you're talking to? And how words ending in こ refer to places? meaningMnemonic: This word ends in い , meaning you know it's probably an adjective. In fact, it ends in しい , which makes it even more likely it's an adjective. Since the kanji 苦 means suffering , this word is the adjective version of that: painful . 苦しい usually describes a painful or distressing feeling that's ongoing and hard to endure, rather than a physical sensation of pain. For example, you can use 苦しい when it's hard to breathe, when you feel emotional pain, or even when your finances are strained .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Everything is really painful right now. Why? You have something heavy on top of you, cru shing ( くる ) you.

meaningMnemonic: The sound that departs from your mouth is you talking. Imagine yourself saying things and words departing your mouth. They are bent in different ways and have different colors, highlighting your pronunciation of certain words and phrases.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 「Otolaryngology」の発音を教えてくれませんか？
sentences.english: Can you tell me the pronunciation of "Otolaryngology"?

sentences.japanese: 先生がLとRの発音を正してくれてからは、上手に発音出来るようになりました。
sentences.english: After the teacher corrected my pronunciation of L and R, I became able to pronounce them well.

sentences.japanese: スピーキング力を上げるため、発音のトレーニングをしています。
sentences.english: I am training in pronunciation to improve my speaking skills.

meaningMnemonic: Things that make your heart strong are reassuring and heartening to hear. You can practically feel your heart becoming stronger in your chest.
readingMnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You learned them when you learned the words 心 and 強い , so you should be able to read this on your own. Just note that つよい gets rendaku'd to づよい !

sentences.japanese: これは心強いデータですね！
プロのプレイヤーがパートナーになってくれるなんて、心強いです。
sentences.english: It's reassuring to have a professional player as my partner.

sentences.japanese: 先生の助言は、私たち学生にとって心強いサポートとなりました。
sentences.english: The teacher's advice became a reassuring support for our students.

meaningMnemonic: You know 事 means "occurrence," but it can also mean "matter." And if you return the matter to another person, you're giving a reply or response .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 今日は、メールの返事が来なかった。
sentences.english: Today, I didn't get a reply to my email.

sentences.japanese: もう少し時間をくれませんか？返事をする前によく考えたいんです。
sentences.english: Would you like to give me a little more time? I want to think it over before I respond.

sentences.japanese: プロポーズの返事が一年以上ないんですが、どうしたらいいですか？
sentences.english: There has been no response to my proposal for over a year, what should I do?

meaningMnemonic: They dwell here, these people . So what are they? They’re residents .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: この町の住民は、おばあちゃんとおじいちゃんが多いです。
sentences.english: Many residents in this town are grandmas and grandpas.

sentences.japanese: アパートの住民たちで、ピザパーティをしたいんです。
sentences.english: I want to have a pizza party with the residents of the apartment.

sentences.japanese: ２０１１年のつなみでは多くの住民が家を失いました。
sentences.english: Many residents lost their homes in the 2011 tsunami.

meaningMnemonic: If you have a part of a roof , that part is your room . Just imagine a roof divided into sections in a house, with the sections going all the way down to the ground. Each section is its own room, right?
readingMnemonic: 部屋 is a bit tricky because it's one of the few Japanese words that use the へ reading for 部 . You'll just have to remember this one is special. Here's a mnemonic to help you out: Imagine you're renting out a room , but all you hear at night is a constant " heh ( へ )… heh... heh... hehehe". An incessant snickering, coming from somewhere inside your room. Hehehe.

sentences.english: to be in a room, to be in one's room
