sentences.english: There's a bed in my room.

sentences.japanese: 南を向いた部屋なので、日当たりがすごくいいんです。
sentences.english: The room is facing south, so it gets good sunlight.

sentences.japanese: 今日の午後は部屋のクリーニングをする予定です。
sentences.english: I plan to clean the room this afternoon.

meaningMnemonic: You want things to depart from your store so you have to sell them. You put all these things up for sale . You are selling these items.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 今日から「手作りチーズケーキ」の発売です！
sentences.english: "Handmade Cheesecake" is on sale starting today!

sentences.japanese: ファンのみんなにお知らせです。私たちのグッズが先ずはオンラインで発売されることになりました。
sentences.english: This is an announcement to all our fans. Our merchandise will be released online first.

sentences.japanese: 私の姉は、新しいスマートフォン発売の十二時間前から、お店の前にいます。
sentences.english: My sister has been in front of the store since twelve hours before the release of the new smartphone.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how 米国 means "America" (the country)? The 米 kanji can actually be used for either of the American continents. In this word we have south combining with America , so it must mean… South America !
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You haven't seen the 南 reading ( なん ), so here's a mnemonic to help you out: In South America everyone eats naan ( なん ). You may be surprised, since naan isn't exactly considered South American food. But what is a flour tortilla, really? It's South American naan!

sentences.japanese: ペルーは南米の国の一つです。
sentences.english: Peru is one of the countries in South America.

sentences.japanese: 学生時代に、バックパッカーとして南米に行きました。
sentences.english: When I was a student, I went to South America as a backpacker.

sentences.japanese: 南米は決して米国の一部ではありませんよ！
sentences.english: South America is by no means a part of the United States!

meaningMnemonic: A south wind is… a south wind ! 南風 is a wind that blows from the south. In Japan it's associated with the warmer temperatures it carries up from the tropics.
readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji, which you've seen before. The かぜ reading is the same one you learned with the vocab word 風 , so if you can remember that you should have no trouble with this word!

sentences.japanese: あたたかい南風がふいています。
sentences.english: A warm southerly wind is blowing.

sentences.japanese: 南風で花がゆれています。
sentences.english: The flowers are swaying in the south wind.

sentences.japanese: 今日は南風が気もちいいです。
sentences.english: The south wind feels nice today.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. That being said, this can also mean difficult or painful , often in a psychological sense, though it can be physical as well. I guess if you're in a spicy situation it's going to be a difficult one.
readingMnemonic: Depending on the context, the reading for this word could be からい or つらい . The からい reading is the spicy one that you learned with the kanji, which you can remember because spicy foods give a から て chop to your mouth. The つらい reading is the difficult or painful one. You can remember this because two Ra s ( つら ) are way more difficult to deal with than one Ra.

sentences.english: this is spicy, this is hard
something is hard to look at
to become spicy, to come to feel hard
to feel that something is hard

sentences.japanese: 「やばい〜！めっちゃ辛い～！でも、このカレーすっげ〜美味しい！」
sentences.english: "Omg! My mouth is on fire, but this curry is sooo good!"

sentences.japanese: 私、辛いものは食べれないんです。
え、そんなことがあったの？それは辛いね。
sentences.english: Oh, that's what happened? That's tough.

meaningMnemonic: If you put something spicy in your mouth you'll end up with a spicy taste or a dry taste in there. Spice sucks up all your mouth moistness.
readingMnemonic: This is the kun'yomi readings together. You should have learned them both by now.

sentences.japanese: カレーはいつも辛口を買います。
sentences.english: When I buy curry, I always buy the spicy kind.

sentences.japanese: アサヒスーパードライはシャープなのどごしの辛口ビールです。
sentences.english: Asahi Super Dry is a dry beer that has a sharp, crisp feeling when it goes down your throat.

sentences.japanese: みんなは辛口コメントだったけど、私はこのドラマの大ファンです。
sentences.english: Everyone gave harsh opinions, but I am actually a big fan of this drama.

meaningMnemonic: Your stand location is where you stand. In other words, it's your standpoint , like in a discussion or on an issue. While 立場 can mean a literal standing place, it's almost always used metaphorically — to describe your stance in an argument or the complexities of your position within society, a situation, or a relationship.
readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji. 立 comes from 立ち (the noun form of 立つ ), and you learned the kun'yomi reading for 場 with 場所 . But here's a mnemonic for both in case you need a refresher: A sheep is trying to give you its standpoint on a touchy ( たち ) subject, but all it can do is say " baa " ( ば ). You're starting to get really offended that it's not baa-thering to take a more nuanced standpoint on such a touchy issue!

sentences.japanese: この家では父が弱い立場にいます。
sentences.english: In this house, the father is in a weak position.

sentences.japanese: 私はそんなこと言える立場じゃありません。
sentences.english: I'm not in a position to say such things.

sentences.japanese: ユーザーの立場から言うと、このアプリは高すぎます。
sentences.english: From a user's standpoint, this app is too expensive.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Did you know the Aries cluster of star s used to be called the Hoe Shee p ( ほし ) constellation? Nah, I'm only messing, but Aries is represented by a ram and actually looks a little like a hoe. And hey, "hoe sheep" sounds like ほし . So, you know, don't let the truth get in the way of a good story.

sentences.japanese: 夜には、星がとてもきれいでした。
sentences.english: That night the stars were really pretty.

sentences.japanese: 青森には美しい星空が広がっています。
sentences.english: A beautiful starry sky stretches over Aomori.

sentences.japanese: フルーツをハート形や星形に切るとかわいいし、小さい子にも人気ですよ。
sentences.english: Fruits cut into heart and star shapes are cute, and popular with children.

meaningMnemonic: You'll see this attached to other words... like "meat" or "fish." When you see this, you'll know it is a ___ store, making this word mean store (same as the kanji).
readingMnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi reading. Don't type the 〜 out when writing the answer. It's just there to let you know that there's usually something attached to this word.

sentences.japanese: 小さい時は、大人になったらケーキ屋さんになりたいと思ってました。
sentences.english: When I was little, I wanted to work in a cake shop when I became an adult.

sentences.japanese: この町には有名なとんこつラーメン屋があります。
sentences.english: There is a famous tonkotsu ramen shop in this town.

sentences.japanese: この前、パン屋で会った男の人に電話番号をきかれたんです。
sentences.english: The other day, a man I met at the bakery asked me for my phone number.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji itself means temporary . When you add the に , we're asking you to imagine a situation temporarily, so the meaning changes to supposing or if .
readingMnemonic: The reading is kun'yomi, so here's a mnemonic to remember it: If you don't mind, could you carry ( かり ) this for me? Supposing it's not too much trouble, of course.

sentences.japanese: 仮に明日雨だったら、ピクニックは中止になる。
sentences.english: Supposing it rains tomorrow, the picnic will be canceled.

sentences.japanese: 仮に大学に入学できなかったら、父の会社に入社するのも一つの手だと思っています。
sentences.english: Hypothetically, if I can't enter university, I think joining my father's company is also an option.

sentences.japanese: 仮に、このベッドが草で出来ていたとしたら、牛たちに食べられてしまったかもしれないよ。
sentences.english: If this bed was made of grass, it might have been eaten by cows.

meaningMnemonic: A certain win sounds like a great thing. When these two kanji are put together, a certain victory is inevitable.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Take note that the つ in ひつ is turned into a small っ , though.

sentences.english: the one who strikes first decides the battle

sentences.japanese: プロポーズ必勝の本が今年のベストセラーになりそうです。
sentences.english: The book about successful marriage proposals is likely to be a bestseller this year.

sentences.japanese: 姉は必勝すると思い、宝くじに二百万円もつかった。
sentences.english: Thinking she would definitely win, my sister spent 2,000,000 yen on the lottery.

sentences.japanese: この『パチンコ必勝マニュアル』で本当に勝てるのでしょうか？
sentences.english: Can I really win if I use this "Pachinko Surefire Win Manual"?

meaningMnemonic: This is the noun version of the kanji swim , so it means swimming .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already so you should be able to read it!

sentences.english: to teach someone how to swim

sentences.japanese: マイケルは魚よりも泳ぎが上手です。
sentences.english: Michael's swimming is better than the fish's!

sentences.japanese: プロの先生に泳ぎのフォームを正してほしいです。
sentences.english: I want a professional instructor to correct my swimming form.

sentences.japanese: すばらしい泳ぎでしたよ。

meaningMnemonic: Your eye is on what's next . How is this possible to see what's coming up? That's because you're looking at a table of contents .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses on'yomi readings of the kanji. You've seen them before, but the もく reading for 目 is still pretty new, so here's a mnemonic: You always provide a table of contents when you mock ( もく ) someone. Your mockery tends to be complicated and go on for a long time, like you're some kind of roast comedian or something, so it helps to distribute a table of contents to the people you're mocking. They really appreciate it.

sentences.english: table of contents for the manual
table of contents for the book
table of contents for the textbook
to look at the table of contents
to read the table of contents
to create a table of contents

sentences.japanese: 先ず、本の目次を見て下さい。
sentences.english: First, please look at the table of contents of the book.

sentences.japanese: 目次を見るだけでも、本の中について少し分かりますよ。
sentences.english: Even just looking at the table of contents tells you a little about the book.

sentences.japanese: 次は、目次のページです。
sentences.english: Next is a page for the table of contents.

meaningMnemonic: This word is almost the same as the kanji, but only half of it. It means tag or amulet . They're about the same shape and size as money, but you can't buy a house with them (...probably).
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: You can't find your tag anywhere. It was just there, you swear, but now it's nowhere to be found. You search for it everywhere, then you realize... it was right there all along. Seriously? You're such a foo l, duh ( ふだ )!

sentences.english: to take a label, to take a playing card

sentences.japanese: 村の入り口にお札がたくさんありました。
sentences.english: There were many amulets at the entrance of the village.

sentences.japanese: 自分の札を見せないようにした方がいいよ。
sentences.english: You should be careful not to show your hand.

sentences.japanese: 空室の札がかかってたので、ノックしなかったんです。
sentences.english: I didn't knock because the vacant room tag was hung.

meaningMnemonic: When you accept a test you are taking an exam or taking a test . Good luck! A++++!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.english: to aim to take an exam
to think of taking an exam
taking a middle school entrance exam
taking a high school entrance exam

sentences.japanese: 大学受験のために、毎日勉強しています。
sentences.english: I study every day for university entrance exams.

sentences.japanese: 受験の不安とストレスが大きい一年でした。
sentences.english: It was a year of great anxiety and stress about taking the exams.

sentences.japanese: 受験がうまくいけば、新しいゲームを買ってもらえるんです。
sentences.english: If my exams go well, they'll buy me a new game.

meaningMnemonic: A versus talk is when you sit down with another person and have a talk . As you're talking, it might evolve into a discussion . Or perhaps you're there to have an interview . 対談 is usually a formal discussion between two or more individuals, often organized ahead of time, and with a specific purpose or topic in mind.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 工学と心理学の学者の対談のイベントに行きました。
sentences.english: I went to an event for discussions between engineering and psychology scholars.

sentences.japanese: 先週、有名な作家と天才モダンアーティストとの対談が行われました。
sentences.english: Last week, a discussion was held between a famous writer and a genius modern artist.

sentences.japanese: 今月号には、私の対談がのってるはずです。
sentences.english: This month's issue should have my interview.

meaningMnemonic: If there's a task occurrence , then there's something you have to do, a.k.a. a task or errand . 用事 generally refers to tasks that you personally need to take care of. Often that means errands like buying groceries or paying bills. It could also mean a doctor's appointment, meeting with a friend, or work tasks like attending a meeting and finishing an assignment. It's anything on your list of things to do !
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: その日、大切な用事があります。
sentences.english: On that day, I have important errands.

sentences.japanese: あっ、田中先生。ドン・キホーテに一体何の用事ですか？
sentences.english: Oh, Tanaka-sensei. What business brings you to Don Quijote?

sentences.japanese: すみません。用事を思い出したので、お先に失礼します。
sentences.english: Excuse me. I'm sorry to leave early, but I just remembered there's something I have to do.

meaningMnemonic: This is the noun version of the kanji teach . So it means teaching .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You already learned this reading when you learned 教える , so you should be able to read this word as well.

sentences.japanese: 「毎日全力で生きる」というのは、父からの教えです。
sentences.english: "Living every day to your fullest" is a teaching from my father.

sentences.japanese: それは、すばらしい教えですね。
sentences.english: It's such a great lesson, isn't it?

sentences.japanese: うちの子は、マナーに対する教えが足りず、失礼なことがあったらすみません。
sentences.english: My child has not been taught enough about manners, and I apologize if they have been rude.

meaningMnemonic: A tea shop is a tea shop . Mmm, delicious, delicious tea. Traditionally, a 茶屋 was a Japanese teahouse where travelers could rest and enjoy tea and snacks. These kinds of 茶屋 are less common today, but the term is still often used for cafes or restaurants designed to evoke the charm of historical Japanese teahouses.
readingMnemonic: This word uses the readings you learned with the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: to go to a tea shop
woman working at the tea shop

sentences.japanese: この町には古い茶屋があります。
sentences.english: This town has an old tea house.

sentences.japanese: 茶屋に入って少し休みませんか？
sentences.english: Would you like to go into the teahouse and take a little break?

sentences.japanese: 茶屋の前には竹林があって、赤い和風のパラソルもあります。
sentences.english: There is a bamboo grove in front of the teahouse, and there is also a red Japanese umbrella.

meaningMnemonic: You've got a ten minute interval of time . That simply makes this ten minutes . Note that, as we mentioned on the page for 〜間 , you can omit 間 and this will still mean ten minutes ! You'll especially see this in conversations and more casual contexts.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You do know all of those, but their behaviour is a little different here. 十 ( じゅう ) and 分 ( ～ふん ) together actually turn into じゅっぷん here. This is sometimes the case when using ～分 to mean "minute" in combination with certain numbers, so try to pay attention to this!

sentences.english: can be done in ten minutes

sentences.japanese: ここで十分間休みましょう。
sentences.english: Let's rest here for ten minutes.

sentences.japanese: 十分間だけゲームしていい？
sentences.english: Can I play a game just for ten minutes?

sentences.japanese: 十分間あれば出来ると思いますよ。
sentences.english: I think I can do it if I have ten minutes.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how 表 meant both express and surface ? This expands on the second meaning, making this the front or the surface . 表 refers to the visible, outward-facing side of something, in contrast to the hidden, back side. It's used for surfaces on display, like the front of a building, the face of a coin, the cover of a book, or the top surface of a package.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet though, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You're standing there, staring at the front of this building. You spend some time gazing at it before you realize what it is. " Oh , mote l ( おもて )," you say aloud. The surface of this building really gave it away. "Oh, motel!"

sentences.english: to go outside, to become public
to put something outside, to make something public

sentences.japanese: この紙の表はピンク色にぬってください。
sentences.english: Please paint the front of this paper pink.

sentences.japanese: 十円玉コインの表はどちらですか？
sentences.english: Which side of a ten yen coin is the front?

sentences.japanese: コウイチは、トーフグの社長です。表向きは。
sentences.english: Koichi is the president of Tofugu. Officially speaking, anyway.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how words beginning with そ are either close to the person you're talking to, or fairly close to both of you? And how words ending in こ refer to places? This one's no exception. そこ means there .

sentences.english: to do something up to there

sentences.japanese: そこで先生に会ったよ。
おやつなら、そこにあるよ。
sentences.english: If you're looking for snacks, they're there.

sentences.japanese: そこまで言わなくてもいいじゃない！
sentences.english: You don't have to say so much!

meaningMnemonic: Both kanji mean world , so it should be easy to guess this is a word for the world . It also means society or the universe .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You know the on'yomi reading for 界 , but you didn't learn this on'yomi reading of 世 , so here's a mnemonic to help you remember: What's the most hated vegetable in the world ? Ce lery ( せ ), probably. The world is divided into those who love celery and those who hate celery. Which one are you?

sentences.english: to turn something towards the world

sentences.japanese: 世界は広いから、色々な国に行きたいです。
sentences.english: The world is big, so I want to go to various countries.

sentences.japanese: このドキュメンタリーは全世界で人気の大作になりました。
sentences.english: This documentary has become a popular masterpiece worldwide.

sentences.japanese: アーティストは、自分の世界を持ってる人が多いです。
sentences.english: Many artists have a world of their own.

meaningMnemonic: Just like the kanji, this means thing . With 物 , we're usually talking about the physical variety of thing — you know, like an object or item .
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading, but you haven't learned it yet. Here's a mnemonic to help you: What game has the most thing s in it? Mono poly ( もの ). You can choose from a bunch of random things to play as, you know? And no one actually knows what those things are. What's a thimble anyway? Just call it a thing.

sentences.english: a thing goes in, things fit
there is a thing, there are things

sentences.japanese: この家には物がありすぎます。
sentences.english: There are too many things in this house.

sentences.japanese: 明日食べる物がないので、スーパーに買いに行ってきます。
sentences.english: We don't have food for tomorrow, so I'm going to the supermarket.

sentences.japanese: 先日、一年前に失くした物を見つけたんです。
sentences.english: The other day, I found something I lost a year ago.

meaningMnemonic: Just like the kanji, this means thing , matter , or occurrence . Unlike 物 , which is typically used for physical objects, 事 usually refers to "things" in the abstract or intangible sense. So, you'll see it in phrases like いい事 (a good thing), する事 (things to do), or 大切な事 (an important matter).
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned that reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you out: You've done all kinds of thing s in your coat ( こと ). If you think about it, you only wear a coat when you have things to do. Try to remember all the things you've done in a coat. It's a lot! Symbolically, your coat = all the things and occurrence s you've experienced, and all the matter s you've had to deal with in life.

sentences.japanese: その事については、後でまたゆっくり話しませんか。
sentences.english: Shall we talk about the matter later?

sentences.japanese: 先生が言ってる事は半分しか分かりませんでした。
sentences.english: I only understood half of what the teacher was saying.

sentences.japanese: 車で会社に行く事が歩いて行く事よりも多いです。
sentences.english: I go to work by car more often than I walk.

meaningMnemonic: In the now occurrence you'll learn your kanji, no? This word means this time . Despite being "this time" it has the feeling of next time , though. It's like saying "okay, this time we'll get it" where "this time" really means "next time," making it a little bit different from 今回 .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: じゃあ、やっぱり今度にしよう。
sentences.english: Okay, then let’s do it next time.

sentences.japanese: 今度、友人と花見に行く予定です。
sentences.english: I'm planning to go see the cherry blossoms with my friends this time.

sentences.japanese: 今度の夏休みは四国に行くつもりです。
sentences.english: This summer vacation I'm going to Shikoku.

meaningMnemonic: You know that the word 付ける means "to attach" and you know that the kanji 付 means attach . So, this word probably has something to do with attaching. This is the intransitive version, though, where something is attached (and you're not doing the attaching). You can use the く as a hint. You see something attached on the wall. You say "Coo'."
readingMnemonic: The reading can be derived from 付ける , a word you should have seen a few levels ago. If you know that word's reading you should be able to figure out this word's reading as well (and vice versa).

sentences.english: to master, to become accustomed to
to be attachable to a car

sentences.japanese: この手紙には、まだ切手が付いてないですよ。
sentences.english: There's no stamp attached to this letter yet.

sentences.japanese: あーあ。白いティシャツにケチャップが付いちゃった。
sentences.english: Ugh, some ketchup got on my white tee shirt.

sentences.japanese: あなたの耳たぶに付いてるそれ、何？
sentences.english: What’s that thing attached to your earlobe?

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means both music and bend . For this word, we're looking at "bend." So the verb 曲がる is to be bent . It's intransitive, so don't give it a direct object. Use it to say something gets bent or bends: a knee is bent, the road bends — that sort of thing. Verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある , it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You already learned this reading with 曲げる , so you should be good to go!

sentences.japanese: この道を右に曲がると、コンビニがあります。
sentences.english: Turn right on this road and you'll find a convenience store.

sentences.japanese: 足首が曲がっている気がするんです。
sentences.english: I feel like my ankle is bent.

sentences.japanese: そのマスタード色のネクタイ、ちょっと曲がってるよ。
sentences.english: Your mustard-colored necktie is a bit crooked.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means below , so you can guess the direction this movement verb takes: this is to descend , or to go down . As a movement verb, it usually describes a gradual downward movement. For example, you'd use this verb to describe walking down a mountain, driving down a hill, or going down a river in a boat.
readingMnemonic: This verb uses the exceptional reading that 下さい also uses. So just replace the さい with る and you're good to go!

sentences.english: to go back the way one came
to descend in a zigzag manner

sentences.japanese: あとはそのまま来た道を下るだけだ。
sentences.english: After that, we just go back down the way we came.

sentences.english: A man riding a skateboard zoomed down the mountain.

sentences.english: In Japan, there is a concept of referring to going north as "ascending" and going south as "descending."

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means express and the verb vocab version is transitive, meaning that it's done to something. So this verb means to express something or to show something .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You're struggling to express something to your friends: namely, that you are a wa lrus ( あらわ ). All your friends think you're a human, so they'll be shocked when you express to them the fact that, actually, you are a walrus. You need to get it off your chest though… Your big, blubbery walrus chest.

sentences.japanese: この赤い玉は、「日の丸」と言って、日の出を表しています。
sentences.english: This red ball is called "hinomaru," and represents the sunrise.

sentences.japanese: 先生へのお礼を表すために、クッキーを作ったんです。
sentences.english: I made cookies to express my thanks to you, Sensei.

meaningMnemonic: You know that 付ける means "to attach" and that 見 means "see." So, when you attach your seeing to something, it's like you're looking around trying to find something. When you find what you're looking for, imagine your eyeballs flying out and attaching to that item, then yelling "I FOUND IT!" You'll usually see this word with the 付 in kana, so 見つける .
readingMnemonic: The readings come from 見る and 付ける . If you use those readings, you'll be able to read this word too.

sentences.japanese: 私の母を見付けることが出来ますか？
先日、あの木の下で宝石を見付けたんです。
sentences.english: The other day, I found a gem under that tree.

sentences.japanese: 今日は、自分の気に入った本を見付けることが出来たので、よかったです。
sentences.english: I was glad I could find a book I like today.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means lack , and this verb has a few meanings related to that. You'll often see it meaning to get chipped , like when talking about a teacup or your teeth. I guess a chipped teacup is lacking... a piece of itself? 欠ける can also literally mean to be lacking , as in "a good goalie is lacking from their team." You can use it like this when you're short of something, or when something is missing that would complete a set. In these situations, you'll usually see it as 欠けている !
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Something is lacking... it's a ca r ( か ). You can't stop thinking about this because you have to walk 40 miles to get to your destination. If only that car wasn't missing, this would be easier. Imagine the sweat... the pain... the thirst... all because that car's not present.

sentences.japanese: マグカップの口の所が欠けてしまった。
sentences.english: The mouth of the mug is chipped.

sentences.japanese: 夕べの月、少しだけ欠けてましたね。
sentences.english: The moon was a little bit less than full last night.

sentences.japanese: うちのおじいちゃんは、よくデリカシーに欠ける失礼な事を言います。
sentences.english: My grandpa often says things that are rude and lacking in delicacy.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means hold and the verb version is to hold something , to carry something , to own something , or to keep something . This is a transitive verb, meaning it takes a direct object. You hold something, like chopsticks, have something, like power, or keep something, like your friend's book over the weekend.
readingMnemonic: If you try to hold something in your hand long enough it will mo ld ( も ). And then that mold will cover your hand, then your arm, then your entire body. Basically, you should never hold anything for too long or you'll become a mold person.

sentences.english: to hold in one's right hand

sentences.japanese: 三十才になるまでに自分の車を持つと決めたんです。
sentences.english: I decided to have my own car before I turned thirty.

sentences.japanese: あの男、左手に何を持ってるんですか？
sentences.english: What is that man holding in his left hand?

sentences.japanese: 夏に出かけるときは、水とタオルを必ず持っていきましょう。
sentences.english: When you go out in the summer, be sure to carry water and a towel.

meaningMnemonic: You know that the kanji means mix and the word 交ぜる means "to mix," so it probably has something to do with that. This word means to intersect , which is kind of like mixing. When two things intersect with each other, they're getting mixed up, so that's where this word gets its meaning. To remember that this one means "to intersect," remember the わ as wa lk. You're walking around, and then you intersect with some people on the street.
readingMnemonic: The reading is almost the same as 交ぜる which you should be familiar with by now. It has the ま but it also has an extra じ in there. That じ is there because you intersect with a group of mage s ( まじ ) that catch you on fire as you walk past.

sentences.japanese: パーティで色々な人と交わるのが下手なんです。
sentences.english: I'm not good at mingling with various people at parties.

sentences.japanese: 二つの道が交わって、ここで一つの道になります。
sentences.english: The two roads intersect and become one road here.

sentences.japanese: トーフグは、アメリカと日本の文化が交わった会社です。
sentences.english: Tofugu is a company where American and Japanese culture mingle.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. You already learned that 通る means "to pass through" or "to pass by," but this is a little different. You aren't the one passing, Sue ( す ) is. So you have to let Sue pass. In other words, this verb is transitive, meaning it has an object. That's why it means to let something pass or to put something through . The way this verb is translated into English changes a lot depending on the noun it's paired with. For example 火を通す is literally "to let the fire pass through," and means "to heat through." 針に糸を通す is literally "to put thread through a needle," so it means "to thread a needle."
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading when you learned 通る . Switch the る for a す and you'll be all set!

sentences.english: to pass a thread through, to thread something
to have a look at, to skim (a document, etc.)
to show someone into the president's office
to show someone into a room
to pass something through a bead (string, etc.)

sentences.japanese: ガラスは光を通します。
sentences.english: Glass lets light pass through it.

sentences.japanese: お肉には、しっかり火を通してください。
会ったばかりの他人を家に通しちゃダメです。
sentences.english: Never let strangers who you just met into your home.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means lose so the verb vocab version means to lose .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You lose your tournament/soccer game/whatever (you decide something applicable to you). You're sad about this. Who's there to comfort you? Your Ma ( ま ). She's a nice lady.

sentences.english: to lose to people, to be outdone by other people

sentences.japanese: 兄は、いつも負けることを不安に思っています。
sentences.english: My brother is always worried about losing.

sentences.japanese: 体は負けても、心は負けないで。
sentences.english: Even if you lose with your body, don't lose with your heart.

sentences.english: "What should we eat?" "It's your call. I lost in rock-paper-scissors."

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means need and the verb vocab version is to need . This one's a little tricky, because although it's usually translated as "to need" in English, it's used more like to be needed or to be necessary . That is, it's an intransitive verb in Japanese, so it doesn't take a direct object.
readingMnemonic: Since the reading isn't like the one you learned, think about what you are going to need ... like, what you're really going to need, more than anything. Then, think of an ea gle, because you really need an eagle. You'll need to come up with the reason why you need an eagle though, so hopefully it's a good one.

sentences.japanese: 考えるのに、もっと時間が要る。
sentences.english: I need more time to think.

sentences.japanese: これは要る物と要らない物のリストです。
sentences.english: This is a list of things you need and what you don't need.

meaningMnemonic: The tool s you use on the road of life are important to have. What is your most important tool ?
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: まずは、ペンや紙などの道具が必要です。
sentences.english: First, you need tools like a pen and paper.

sentences.japanese: それは科学実験のための道具です。

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means preserve and the verb vocab version is to preserve something , to keep something , or to maintain something . This is a transitive verb, so it takes a direct object. You preserve something, like your youth.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: If you want to learn how to preserve something like fruits and veggies, you should start with tamots ( たも ), that's slang for delish tomatoes. Once they're preserved, you get to make everyone you love eat those yummy tamots. Mmm!

sentences.japanese: 体力を保つには毎日トレーニングしなくてはいけません。
sentences.english: To keep your physical strength, you have to train every day.

sentences.japanese: 元気な心を保つために、ヨガやメディテーションをします。
sentences.english: I do yoga and meditation to maintain a healthy heart.

sentences.japanese: ヘルシーな生活を送って、今の体重を保ちたいと思います。
sentences.english: I want to live a healthy life and maintain my current weight.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means receive , and this verb means just about the same thing: to receive something ! This is a transitive verb, so it takes a direct object. But 受ける often implies passive reception, generally of intangible objects like an education, or damage. It can also mean to take something , like taking an exam or a job offer.
readingMnemonic: There’s a creature in front of you that’s about to receive something , but what is it? It’s an u ni ( う ), and it’s going to receive a warm welcome and an education. Picture the sea urchin receiving these things, and then going on to take an exam to prove how much education it’s received.

sentences.japanese: 明日、先生から電話を受ける。
sentences.english: I will receive a phone call from my teacher tomorrow.

sentences.japanese: 今回はJLPTの試験を冬に受ける事にしました。
sentences.english: This time, I decided to take the JLPT exam in winter.

sentences.japanese: 他人から言われた事を、毎回まともに受けなくてもいいんだよ。
sentences.english: You don't have to take what others say seriously every time.

meaningMnemonic: You know that 受ける means "to receive something." Combine it with 取る (to take something), and 受け取る … still means to receive something . However, while 受ける generally implies passive reception, 受け取る carries a stronger connotation of actively taking possession of something. It is used when receiving a package or gift, or even when interpreting someone's words as having a specific meaning, such as an insult or compliment.
readingMnemonic: If you know how to read 受ける and 取る , you should be good to go.

sentences.japanese: 海外から年金を受け取る方法ってありますか？
sentences.english: Is there a way to receive a pension from overseas?

sentences.english: I haven't received my ticket yet, even though I'm leaving tomorrow.

sentences.japanese: 家にいるから、アマゾンのパッケージ、代わりに受け取っておくよ。
sentences.english: Since I'm at home, I'll receive the Amazon package on your behalf.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means return so the verb version means to return something . This is more like "to return a thing" rather than returning home, which would be 帰る , a word you haven't seen yet (but will soon, I'm sure!).
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You have to return the Ca r e gg ( かえ ) you found on the side of the road. It will birth a little car, but it needs its mother. So, you try to figure out how to return it. Go ahead and think through that process in your mind. Also think about how weird a car egg would be.

sentences.english: to return to face up, to turn right side out (sewing)

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means ride so the verb vocab version means to ride .
readingMnemonic: The reading is kun'yomi (see that hiragana?) but that's the reading you learned with the kanji. Enjoy the ride!

sentences.english: The dog on that surfboard is cute!

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means sell , and this is a transitive verb meaning to sell something .

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means send , and the vocab verb version is to send something . If the object of this verb is a person, it means "to send" in the sense of to escort someone , maybe to the station, or to the door.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means swim so the verb vocab version is to swim .
readingMnemonic: The reading is kun'yomi (see that hiragana sticking out?) but that's the reading you learned with the kanji.

sentences.japanese: 台風が近づいてるので、海で泳ぐのは安全ではありません。

sentences.japanese: あんた、目が泳いでるよ。

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. sentences.japanese: インタビューを試みる

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means win so the verb version is to win .

meaningMnemonic: If you go far enough south , every country is a tropical country . Well, relative to Japan anyway… Probably different if you live in the southern hemisphere. In Japanese, 南国 often refers to tropical countries or islands like Thailand, Guam, and Hawaii. Sometimes it can refer to the warmer southern regions of Japan as well, like Okinawa.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses on'yomi readings for 南 ( なん ) and 国 ( こく , but rendaku'd to ごく here). You've seen those readings before, but the なん reading is still pretty new, so here's a mnemonic just in case: When you're in a tropical country , you always get a craving for naan ( なん ) bread. You could be in any southern country with a warm, tropical climate — for some reason the heat just makes you want to nosh on some naan.

to come to a southern country
to live in a tropical country

sentences.english: Tropical countries are warm all year round.

meaningMnemonic: The truth behind someone's strength is their true strength . It is also their true ability .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 力 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: Your true strength is sealed behind two locks. Gee, two lock s ( じつりょく )?! People must have been scared of your true power to seal it behind two locks!

sentences.japanese: 全ての実力を出しても、同点の引き分けでした。
sentences.english: Even if I used all of my true strength, it was still a draw.

sentences.japanese: 弟は実力があるのに、なぜプロになれないのか不安に思っているようです。
sentences.english: The younger brother seems to be worried about why he cannot be a professional, despite his true strength.

sentences.japanese: コウイチのフラダンスの実力は本物です。
sentences.english: Koichi's hula dancing abilities are genuine.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the on'yomi reading, same like you learned with the kanji. That is the truth, I promise.

sentences.english: As a matter of fact, I've been on the Olympics even though I may not look like it.

meaningMnemonic: A weak insect . This is what people call weakling s in Japan. This is a good word to know if you're a bully, or something.
readingMnemonic: The reading for this one is a weird one. It uses the kun'yomi readings for both, meaning you'll have to pull your knowledge of the word 弱い from earlier and apply it here. 虫 should be okay, though, as this is the reading you learned with the kanji. Just remember, only weak bugs use kun'yomi, and that weak bug is you in this instance.

sentences.japanese: 弟は弱虫だと言われている。
sentences.english: People say my younger brother is a wimp.

sentences.japanese: 気は強いけど、ちょっと弱虫な男がタイプです。
sentences.english: My type is a man with a strong will but is a bit wimpy.

sentences.japanese: 弱虫だって毛虫だってなんだって、君は君のままでいいよ。
sentences.english: No matter what you are — whether you're a wimp, or even a caterpillar, you should be just the way you are.

meaningMnemonic: Something that is double weak is probably pretty weak. You also know that this is an adjective because it ends with い . You know that 弱い is weak, so it probably isn't that. Instead, this one is weak looking or frail . If you know the grammar らしい you can kind of use that as a hint. The しい on the end reminds me of らしい which is like "seems to be." So, "seems to be weak" = "weak looking."
readingMnemonic: The reading is double kun'yomi, as you can probably guess due to all the hiragana involved. So, you double up on よわ and then add the しい to read this vocabulary word.

sentences.english: My husband ran with all his might, despite his weak-looking body.

sentences.english: My mother in a weak voice told her grandmother, "Take time to rest."
